title: India's Semiconductor Market to Hit $200 Billion by 2035 as Five Plants Go Live: EY-IESA
excerpt: The EY-IESA report unveiled at SEMICON India 2026 projects threefold growth as commercial chip production begins at five units, including new lines at Mohali and Surat.
body:
• India's semiconductor market is projected to grow more than threefold from nearly $64 billion in 2026 to $200 billion by 2035, according to the EY-IESA report unveiled at SEMICON India 2026.
  • Five commercial chip units are now operational — Micron, Kaynes Semicon and CG Semi, plus new production lines at CDIL Semiconductor in Mohali and Suchi Semicon in Surat inaugurated virtually by Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
  • Consumer electronics (30%), automotive (16%) and industrial applications (15%) drive demand; India's chip imports have grown fivefold since FY17 to $30.3 billion in FY25.
  • India houses nearly 20% of the world's chip design engineers, the talent base the industry says will scale domestic design and manufacturing.

From ambition to action

India's semiconductor story has crossed an important threshold. "The semiconductor story in India has moved from ambition to action, from announcements to commercial production — and from individual projects to an ecosystem," Ashok Chandak, president of SEMI India and the India Electronics and Semiconductor Association (IESA), said at SEMICON India 2026 in New Delhi. The gathering marked the point where India's chip strategy shifted from laying policy foundations to building manufacturing capacity, localising the supply chain, and developing indigenous design capabilities.

The headline number comes from the report Semicon India 2.0: From capacity creation to ecosystem leadership, produced by EY and IESA. It projects India's chip market growing at a blistering clip, powered by artificial intelligence, data centres, telecommunications, electric mobility and advanced manufacturing — sectors creating entirely new avenues of demand.

Five plants running

The report's launch coincided with a concrete milestone: commercial production lines at CDIL Semiconductor in Mohali and Suchi Semicon in Surat were inaugurated virtually by the Prime Minister, taking the number of operational commercial semiconductor ATMP (assembly, testing, marking and packaging) units under Semicon 1.0 to five — alongside Micron, Kaynes Semicon and CG Semi.

That makes the narrative an ecosystem story rather than a collection of individual fabs, Chandak argued: capabilities now span design and IP, advanced packaging, equipment, materials, logistics, talent and electronics manufacturing. "India is moving from credibility to capability, with investments increasingly translating into manufacturing, partnerships and commercialisation."

The demand engine

The economics are compelling. Consumer electronics alone accounts for 30% of India's semiconductor market, followed by automotive at 16% and industrial applications at 15%. Meanwhile India's chip imports have expanded more than fivefold, from $5.7 billion in FY17 to $30.3 billion in FY25 — a 23% compound annual growth rate that shows domestic consumption is already there. The question the industry is betting on is whether that consumption can be converted into local fabrication instead of imports.

The trump card is people. India accounts for nearly 20% of the world's chip design engineers, a talent pool the report calls the foundation for scaling manufacturing, indigenous design and commercialisation. As Chandak put it: "The next phase will be defined by execution, innovation, technology commercialisation, indigenous IP, specialised talent, and ecosystem depth."

"India has moved beyond semiconductor ambition. The opportunity now is to build an ecosystem that the world trusts, India owns and the next generation can scale."

— Ashok Chandak, President, IESA

Diaspora angle

For the large Indian engineering community in the US and elsewhere — many working in chip design at firms that now want India as a second base — the $200 billion projection is a career map. It means design centres, fab projects and supply-chain jobs that didn't exist three years ago, and a reason to watch where the next ATMP and fab announcements land.

What's next

The report's own framing is the honest one: capacity creation is done, ecosystem leadership is not. The industry's test over the next decade is execution — turning five packaging plants and a design-engineering advantage into the deep supply chain of materials, equipment and IP that a $200 billion market requires.
